content.heading: 9.0  Making an agent seem to remember
content.body:
Two facts from earlier chapters set up a problem: the LLM is stateless (Chapter 2) and its context window — its "desk" — is finite (Chapter 2). Yet useful agents must remember conversations, recall a user's preferences, and stay coherent over long interactions.

This chapter is about MEMORY: the kinds of memory an agent can have, how we manage the limited desk over time, and how "remembering across runs" actually works. It sets up the next two chapters (embeddings and retrieval).
content.callout: The model forgets everything each request. Memory is how we make it seem to remember.

content.heading: 9.1  The problem in one sentence
content.body:
The model forgets everything the instant a request finishes, and it can only hold so much on its desk at once — so how do we make an agent seem to remember, and how do we keep long interactions from overflowing?

The solution shape is always the same, and it is worth stating as a principle: store information OUTSIDE the model, then bring back the RELEVANT part and place it on the desk (in the prompt) when it is needed.

The model's context is the working desk; your storage is the filing cabinet. Memory engineering is largely about deciding what to fetch from the cabinet and lay on the desk for each request, since the desk is small and everything not on it is forgotten the instant the request finishes.
content.callout: Store outside the model; retrieve the relevant slice; place it on the finite desk. This one shape solves both memory and knowledge.

content.heading: 9.2  Kinds of memory
content.body:
It helps to name the different kinds of memory an agent might have. The vocabulary mirrors how people talk about human memory.

SHORT-TERM (or WORKING) MEMORY: the current conversation or task — the running list of messages (Chapter 7). It lasts only for the run and is bounded by the context window.

LONG-TERM MEMORY, which persists across runs, comes in flavors. EPISODIC: memory of past events and interactions ("last week you asked about X"). SEMANTIC: facts and knowledge ("this user is on the Premium plan"). PROCEDURAL: learned know-how and skills (often baked into prompts and tools rather than stored as data).

The Java parallel is clean: short-term memory is like a variable scoped to a single request; long-term memory is like a database you read from and write to across many requests. The model itself has no persistence at all — you provide it, exactly as you would attach a datastore to an otherwise stateless service.

The engineering job, then, is threefold: decide WHAT to remember, decide WHERE to store it, and decide HOW to bring the right slice back onto the finite desk.
content.callout: Working memory is a request-scoped variable; long-term memory is a database you attach to a stateless service.

content.heading: 9.3  Managing the desk — short-term context strategies
content.body:
Long conversations and long agent runs eventually overflow the context window, and — because you resend the history each turn (Chapter 2) — they also cost more with every step. There are a few standard strategies, each with a trade-off.

TRUNCATION (a sliding window): keep only the most recent handful of messages (plus the system prompt), and drop the oldest. Simple, but you risk forgetting something important that was said early on.

SUMMARIZATION: periodically compress the older part of the conversation into a short summary, and replace the original messages with that summary. This preserves the gist while using far fewer tokens. Common in 2026 for long-running agents. The trade-off is that summarizing loses detail — the summary might omit something that later turns out to matter.

OFFLOADING TO EXTERNAL MEMORY: rather than keeping everything on the desk, write important facts to storage (9.4) and fetch them back only when relevant. This is the bridge to retrieval (Chapters 10-11).

KEEPING A COMPACT "STATE" INSTEAD OF THE RAW TRANSCRIPT: maintain a small, structured summary of the important facts or the current plan, and carry THAT along instead of the entire back-and-forth.

The overarching rule: treat the context window as a scarce, expensive resource — more like a cache than a database. Put on the desk only what is relevant for the NEXT step.
content.callout: Treat the context window like a cache, not a database. Put on the desk only what the NEXT step needs.

content.heading: 9.4  Persistent memory — simple forms first
content.body:
Not every memory need calls for something elaborate. It is worth starting simple, because simple often suffices.

PROFILE / KEY-VALUE MEMORY: store a handful of structured facts about the user or session — their name, their plan, their preferences — in ordinary storage (a small record, a file, or a database). At the start of each run, place the relevant facts onto the desk by including them in the system prompt: "This user prefers concise answers and is on the Premium plan."

AN APPEND LOG: keep a running log of past interactions with timestamps, and fetch recent or keyword-matched entries when relevant.

These simple approaches cover a surprising amount of "memory." You only need the more sophisticated machinery of the next chapters — embeddings and semantic search — when you must retrieve by MEANING from a LARGE collection where simple lookups fall short.
content.callout: Start simple. Profiles and logs cover a surprising amount of "memory" before you need embeddings.

content.heading: 9.5  "Context engineering" — a 2026 framing
content.body:
A phrase that gained currency by 2026 is "context engineering" — the deliberate craft of deciding exactly what goes onto the model's desk for each call. It reframes a lot of what this book teaches under one idea: the model's behavior is overwhelmingly shaped by what is in its context RIGHT NOW, so the highest-leverage work is curating that context.

Context engineering includes: the system prompt and instructions (Chapter 4); the relevant slice of conversation history (this chapter); retrieved knowledge from documents (Chapters 10-11); tool descriptions and recent tool results (Chapter 6); and any facts fetched from long-term memory (this chapter).

All of it competes for the same finite desk. So context engineering is a constant balancing act: include what genuinely helps the next step, and leave out what does not — because irrelevant clutter both costs tokens and can actively distract the model. When you hear "context engineering," think: thoughtfully choosing what the model sees, moment to moment.
content.callout: Context engineering: thoughtfully choosing what the model sees, moment to moment. Irrelevant clutter is not harmless.

content.heading: 9.6  Memory for agents, assembled
content.body:
A capable, long-lived agent typically combines several of these ideas at once.

Working memory: the current run's messages, kept manageable with summarization (9.3). Semantic memory: a store of facts about the user or domain, with the relevant bits pulled onto the desk each run. Episodic memory: a log of past sessions, retrievable by recency or by relevance. A deliberate "remember this" ability: you can even give the agent a TOOL (Chapter 6) that lets it choose to save a fact for later — "remember that the user prefers metric units." Now memory itself becomes something the agent can act on, not just something done to it.

Frameworks (Chapter 12) offer ready-made "memory" components, but every one of them is built from these same primitives: store outside the model, retrieve the relevant slice, place it on the desk. Understanding the primitives means no framework's memory feature will mystify you.
content.callout: Every framework's "memory" feature is built from the same primitives: store outside, retrieve the slice, place on the desk.

content.heading: 9.7  Common pitfalls
content.body: REMEMBERING TOO MUCH: stuffing the desk with everything "just in case" wastes tokens and can bury the useful part. Curate. REMEMBERING TOO LITTLE: aggressive truncation can drop a crucial early fact; summarize rather than simply forget when the early context matters. SUMMARIES THAT LOSE THE POINT: a careless summary can omit exactly the detail that later matters; summarize with the goal in mind. PRIVACY AND SENSITIVE DATA: long-term memory may hold personal information; storing and re-injecting it has privacy implications (Chapter 16). MEMORY THAT GOES STALE: a stored fact ("user is on the Free plan") can become wrong over time; decide how memories get updated or expire.
content.callout: Curate, don't hoard. Summarize with the goal in mind. Protect sensitive data. Let stale memories expire.

content.heading: Check your understanding
content.body:
For reflection, not coding.

1. Restate the universal solution shape for both memory and knowledge problems in one sentence.

2. Distinguish short-term (working) memory from long-term memory, and name the three flavors of long-term memory.

3. Compare truncation and summarization for managing a long conversation. What does each risk losing?

4. Give an example of "profile memory" and explain how it gets onto the model's desk for a given run.

5. Explain "context engineering" in your own words, and why irrelevant clutter in the context is not harmless.
